title: The pacemaker of the ice ages
teaches: How slow changes in the Earth's orbit time the ice ages, and how the record was read from deep-sea mud

blocks.text: Soon after Agassiz's ice age was accepted, geologists found that it had been a series of events. In the American Midwest and in the Alps, layers of glacial debris were separated by old soils and peat containing the remains of warm-climate plants, which showed that the ice had advanced, melted away, and advanced again. By the early twentieth century, Albrecht Penck and Eduard Brückner had identified four separate glaciations in the Alps. Any theory of the ice ages now had to explain why the climate should swing back and forth.

In the 1860s and 1870s James Croll, a self-taught Scot who worked as a janitor at Anderson's University in Glasgow and used its library to read physics and astronomy, proposed an astronomical cause. The gravitational pull of the other planets slowly alters the shape of the Earth's orbit and the tilt and orientation of its axis, changing how much sunlight reaches each latitude in each season. Croll's calculations placed the end of the last ice age about 80,000 years ago. When field geologists calculated from the erosion of the Niagara gorge and St Anthony Falls that the ice had left North America only about 10,000 years ago, Croll's theory was set aside.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Glacial debris separated by warm-climate soils and peat shows that the Pleistocene had many glaciations, with warm interglacial periods between them.
James Croll proposed in the 1860s that slow changes in the Earth's orbit drove these cycles, though his calculations placed the last ice age too far in the past.

blocks.text: The idea was revived by Milutin Milanković, a Serbian civil engineer and mathematician. Interned in Budapest during the First World War, where he was allowed to work in the library of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, he spent years calculating by hand how much sunlight each latitude had received in each season over the past several hundred thousand years. He published his early curves in 1920; in 1924 they appeared in a book on ancient climates by the climatologist Wladimir Köppen and his son-in-law, Alfred Wegener of lesson 8, and Milanković brought all his work together in a single volume in 1941.

The Earth's path and posture vary in three ways. The tilt of the axis wobbles between about 22.1° and 24.5° on a cycle of about 41,000 years; a steeper tilt makes summers hotter and winters colder at high latitudes. The shape of the orbit stretches from nearly circular to slightly elliptical and back over cycles of roughly 100,000 and 400,000 years, its **eccentricity** (a measure of how far it departs from a circle) varying between nearly 0 and about 0.06. Meanwhile, the axis itself traces out a slow cone in space, so the point in the orbit where a given season falls creeps around the ellipse, a shift called **precession** that completes a cycle in about 21,000 years. Today the Earth makes its closest approach to the Sun in early January, during the northern winter; about 11,000 years ago it was closest in July.

Following a suggestion of Köppen's, Milanković argued that the decisive quantity was the strength of summer sunshine at high northern latitudes, around 65° N, where the great ice sheets of North America and Europe began. Winters there are always cold enough for snow. Whether an ice sheet starts to grow depends on whether the summer is warm enough to melt the winter's snow before the next winter begins. A long run of mild, weak summers lets snow survive from year to year and pack into ice.

blocks.text: The weakest northern summers occur when the tilt is low, the orbit is strongly stretched, and the Earth passes closest to the Sun in December or January, placing it farthest from the Sun in June. Over the last million years, midsummer sunshine at 65° N has ranged from about 440 to 550 W/m², a swing of roughly 20%, even though the total sunlight the whole Earth receives over a year changes by less than 0.2%. The orbital cycles redistribute sunlight between seasons and between latitudes while leaving the global annual budget almost untouched.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Axial tilt varies over about 41,000 years, orbital eccentricity over about 100,000 and 400,000 years, and the precession of the seasons over about 21,000 years.
Weak summer sunshine around 65° N lets winter snow survive through the melt season and accumulate into ice sheets.
Orbital cycles redistribute sunlight across seasons and latitudes while barely changing the total sunlight the Earth receives in a year.

blocks.text: Testing Milanković's curves required a continuous, dated record of past glaciations. The glacial deposits on land could never provide one, because each new advance of an ice sheet bulldozed away much of the debris left by earlier ones. The unbroken record came instead from the deep ocean floor, where fine clay and the shells of microscopic plankton settle at a few centimetres per thousand years.

Among those shells are those of **foraminifera**, single-celled organisms the size of sand grains that build shells of calcium carbonate. The oxygen in that carbonate comes in two main stable isotopes (lesson 7): common oxygen-16 and heavier oxygen-18. Because water molecules containing lighter oxygen-16 evaporate slightly more readily, the water vapour that travels poleward and falls as snow on ice sheets is depleted in oxygen-18. As continental ice sheets grow, they lock up this isotopically light water on land and leave the remaining ocean slightly enriched in oxygen-18. Foraminifera building their shells from that seawater record its isotopic ratio, mixed with a smaller effect from the temperature of the water itself. Measuring the ratio of oxygen-18 to oxygen-16 in shells layer by layer down a sediment core therefore tracks the volume of ice on land through time.

blocks.caption: The shell of Globigerina, a foraminifer of the open ocean about half a millimetre across, seen under an electron microscope.

blocks.text: Cesare Emiliani published the first oxygen-isotope curves from deep-sea cores in 1955, reading them mainly as a record of ocean temperature; in 1967 Nicholas Shackleton, by analysing foraminifera that lived on the cold, stable sea floor, showed that the swings mostly recorded the growth and melting of the great ice sheets. Hundreds of cores have been measured since. In 2005 Lorraine Lisiecki and Maureen Raymo combined 57 of them into a single reference curve spanning the last 5.3 million years, the LR04 stack shown in the figure below.

blocks.caption: The LR04 deep-sea record (Lisiecki and Raymo, 2005): the oxygen isotopes in foraminifera shells, a measure of the ice on land. Up is less ice. A cycle of the chosen length is laid over it, with a score for how well it fits.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Growing ice sheets lock up water rich in lighter oxygen-16, leaving the oceans enriched in heavier oxygen-18.
The oxygen-isotope ratio in fossil foraminifera shells from deep-sea sediment cores tracks how much ice stood on the continents.
The LR04 stack merges 57 deep-sea cores into a continuous 5.3-million-year record of global ice volume.

blocks.text: In 1976 James Hays, John Imbrie and Nicholas Shackleton analysed two cores from the southern Indian Ocean, dated with the magnetic reversals of lesson 9 and other markers. Breaking the 450,000-year record into its component frequencies, they found three main rhythms: one near 100,000 years, one near 42,000 years, and a pair at 23,000 and 19,000 years. These matched the calculated periods of eccentricity, tilt and precession. Their paper, 'Variations in the Earth's Orbit: Pacemaker of the Ice Ages', settled the long argument in Milanković's favour.

Longer cores later revealed a shift that the 1976 record did not reach. Before about a million years ago, ice sheets waxed and waned every 41,000 years, in step with the tilt of the axis. Over the last 800,000 years the dominant rhythm has been the 100,000-year cycle, marked by slow build-ups of ice that end in abrupt meltings, giving the graph a sawtooth shape. That shift is puzzling because eccentricity, the only orbital cycle with a 100,000-year period, alters summer sunshine at 65° N far less than tilt or precession do. Why the longer rhythm took over, and why each cycle ends so suddenly, is still debated. Most explanations call on the internal dynamics of massive ice sheets, which become unstable once they grow past a certain size and depress the crust beneath them, together with feedbacks in the carbon cycle: cores drilled from the Antarctic ice sheet preserve bubbles of ancient air that show atmospheric carbon dioxide falling during glaciations and rising during melts, amplifying the modest orbital push.

blocks.caption: The last 800,000 years: the Earth's orbit (Laskar and others, 2004), the midsummer sunshine at 65° N it gives, and the ice on land in the LR04 deep-sea record.
blocks.task: Play the last 800,000 years and compare the rhythm of the sunshine with the rhythm of the ice

blocks.text: The orbit sets the timing of the ice ages, while the ice sheets, the oceans and the atmosphere govern the size of the response. During the last glacial maximum, about 21,000 years ago, ice sheets covered much of North America and northern Europe; their retreat brought on the present warm interglacial, the Holocene, about 11,700 years ago. The landforms left behind by that last retreat are the subject of the next lesson.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Deep-sea sediment cores show ice-volume cycles at about 100,000, 41,000, and 23,000 to 19,000 years, matching the periods of eccentricity, tilt and precession.
A 41,000-year cycle dominated until about a million years ago; since about 800,000 years ago, a sawtooth 100,000-year cycle has dominated.
Orbital variations pace the ice ages, while ice-sheet dynamics and greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide amplify the climate response.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the orbit and the ice ages
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: In Milanković's theory, what condition allows a northern ice sheet to start growing?
choices: Cool summers at high northern latitudes that fail to melt all of the previous winter's snow
Exceptionally cold winters at high northern latitudes that produce heavier snowfall
A drop in the total amount of sunlight reaching the Earth over the course of the year
items.why: Winters near 65° N are always cold enough for snow; whether snow accumulates from year to year depends on how much of it survives the summer melt season.

items.ask: Which orbital configuration produces the weakest northern summers?
choices: Low axial tilt, a stretched orbit, and closest approach to the Sun in December (so the Earth is farthest in June)
High axial tilt, a nearly circular orbit, and closest approach to the Sun in June
High axial tilt, a stretched orbit, and closest approach to the Sun in June
items.why: Low tilt reduces summer sunshine at high latitudes, and an eccentric orbit with aphelion (the far point) in June weakens northern summer sunlight further.

items.ask: Why does seawater have a higher ratio of oxygen-18 to oxygen-16 during a glacial maximum?
choices: Water molecules with lighter oxygen-16 evaporate more readily and get trapped in continental ice sheets, leaving heavier oxygen-18 behind in the ocean
Growing ice sheets weather continental rocks and wash extra oxygen-18 into the sea
Colder seawater absorbs more oxygen-18 directly from the atmosphere
items.why: Snow falling on ice sheets is depleted in oxygen-18. Locking that light water up on land leaves the oceans, and the shells grown in them, enriched in oxygen-18.

items.ask: Between 1.2 and 2 million years ago, the LR04 record is dominated by a 41,000-year cycle. Which orbital variation has this period?
choices: The tilt of the Earth's axis
The eccentricity (stretch) of the Earth's orbit
The precession of the seasons around the orbit
items.why: The tilt of the Earth's axis oscillates between about 22.1° and 24.5° on a 41,000-year cycle.

items.ask: Why is the strong 100,000-year glacial cycle of the last 800,000 years considered a puzzle?
choices: The 100,000-year eccentricity cycle changes high-latitude summer sunshine much less than tilt or precession do
No known change in the Earth's orbit has a period near 100,000 years
The 100,000-year cycle appears only in Antarctic ice cores and not in deep-sea sediment
items.why: Eccentricity varies on a ~100,000-year timescale, but its direct effect on insolation is tiny; internal feedbacks from large ice sheets and the carbon cycle must amplify it.

summary: **Earth’s orbit changes in slow cycles.** Tilt (41,000 years), eccentricity (100,000 and 400,000 years) and precession (21,000 years).
**The cycles change summer sunshine at high latitudes.**
**Cool northern summers grow ice sheets.** Winter snow that survives the melt season builds up year after year.
**Deep-sea mud records the ice.** Oxygen isotopes in fossil foraminifera show how much water was locked up on land.
**The ice ages follow the orbit.** A 41,000-year beat until about a million years ago, and a 100,000-year beat since.
**Feedbacks amplify the orbital nudge.** Ice-sheet dynamics and carbon dioxide turn small changes in sunshine into ice ages.
